claims.assertion: The driver cancelled the trip (F4), so the $6.61 cancellation fee can only be justified through the no-show branch of the policy.

NS-1's first requirement is not met: no arrival confirmation exists on the record — the timeline shows driver_pressed_here_at is null, the driver never tapped "I'm Here" and the platform recorded no automatic arrival (F6).

The driver's own written statement confirms the defect: "I forgot to press the I'm Here button but I was there" (F12); a driver's after-the-fact statement cannot substitute for the missing arrival record.
Because a requirement of NS-1 fails, NS-2 applies and the $6.61 cancellation fee charged on the record (F7) must be refunded in full.

The rider was not a no-show in substance: the driver reached the pickup area at 22:41:30 and stayed within 200 m for 5 min 20 s in total (F2), and the driver's own message at 22:43 said he was at the pickup point (F9), while the rider was on her way down to the pickup point.

The rider's profile — 3.4 years on the platform, 4.9 rating, no upheld disputes in 90 days (F16) — supports taking her account at face value, and the driver's profile shows a 90-day dispute history of its own (F17).

weaknesses: The GPS record shows the driver did in fact wait: stationary 22:42:50–22:46:50, 4 min 0 s, 40 m from the pickup point (F3), with a closest approach of 34 m (F1) and 5 min 20 s cumulative within 200 m (F2). The driver will argue that the substance of NS-1 (ii) and (iii) is satisfied and that the only failure is the button, which his statement (F12) admits but characterises as harmless.

The driver's message at 22:43 placing himself at the pickup (F9) and the timeline's recorded arrival at 22:41:30 (F5) cut against any suggestion that he never reached the rider, so the case cannot be built on non-arrival; it must rest on the missing NS-1 (i) record (F6).

The rider's complaint gives no evidence of exactly when she would have reached the pickup point, and there is no GPS or timeline fact showing her position after 22:41:30, so she cannot show she was arriving within the statutory waiting period; she can only rely on the driver's own non-compliance.

The cancellation fee on record is $6.61 with no surge (F7, F8), so the sum in dispute is small and the only route to recovery is NS-2, which the judge may read narrowly given the driver's undisputed physical presence (F3).

claims.assertion: The pickup location in this case is a large civic/transport complex (Woodlands Civic Centre); the GPS record shows the driver reached and stayed in the immediate vicinity of the pickup point, closest approach 34 m at 22:42:45 (F1), and within 200 m of pickup from 22:41:30 with 5 min 20 s cumulative time inside that radius before cancellation (F2), so the driver did in fact present himself at the pickup point.

The driver waited continuously beyond the three-minute no-show threshold: he was stationary at a point 40 m from the pickup from 22:42:50 to 22:46:50, a full 4 minutes 0 seconds (F3), and the platform timeline independently records arrival at 22:41:30 with cancellation 5 min 20 s later (F5).

The trip was matched at 22:37:00 and cancelled by the driver at 22:46:50, i.e. 9 min 50 s after acceptance (F4); the rider's own complaint admits she was 'on my way down' and never states she arrived at the pickup point or boarded, so the waiting period was consumed by rider delay rather than by any failure on the driver's part.

The driver's in-app messages during the wait were normal and non-confrontational — 'At the pickup point, silver Toyota Altis.' at 22:43 (F9) and 'Waited 4 min, cancelling' at 22:46 (F10) — giving the rider the vehicle identity and a final notice before cancellation; the chat record is complete with every message timestamped (F11), so nothing in the communication suggests the driver abandoned the pickup early or acted in bad faith.

The $6.61 cancellation fee on record (F7) has not been inflated by surge — the multiplier was 1.0x (F8) — so the amount in dispute is exactly the published NS-0 cancellation fee, and if the conditions of NS-1 are met the fee stands unchanged for the rider.

The single procedural gap is the arrival button: the driver never tapped 'I'm Here' and no automatic arrival was recorded (F6), which he explains in his statement as having forgotten the button while physically being at the pickup (F12); where the rider's complaint and the driver's statement conflict, the GPS and timeline records (F1, F2, F3, F5) are the system records and show he was at the pickup and waited in range over four minutes.

The rider is not a habitual complainant and the driver has a long clean record — rider 1 dispute in 90 days, 0 upheld (F16), driver 4.7 years, 4.87 rating, 951 trips in 90 days with 0 disputes upheld (F17) — so a finding of fraud or abuse of the cancellation button against this driver would be inconsistent with the account history, and no such finding is warranted here.

There is no safety dimension to this case: the chat contains no threat, harassment or abuse (F9, F10, F11), and the driver left the scene peacefully after waiting rather than confronting the rider, in line with the guidance that drivers report rather than take matters into their own hands.

weaknesses: NS-1(i) is on its face not satisfied: the record shows the driver never tapped 'I'm Here' and the platform logged no automatic arrival (F6), and the driver himself admits he forgot the button (F12). NS-2 provides that if any of (i)(ii)(iii) fails the $6.61 must be refunded in full, so on the strict text the rider's refund claim is strong.

The 200 m arrival radius relied on in D1 is a data-layer parameter (G2), not a published Ryde rule; the rider will argue 'arrival' required the recorded 'I'm Here' tap, which is absent (F6), and that the driver's statement (F12) is a mere claim that cannot cure a missing system record.

The rider's complaint that she was 'on my way down' cannot be contradicted by any system record of her actual movement — the fact table contains no rider-side GPS or address-log evidence — so the judge may find the driver cancelled while the rider was genuinely en route, which supports the refund even if the driver's conduct was not blameworthy.

The driver's own station is 40 m from the pickup point (F3), not at it; the rider may argue that a 40 m offset in a Woodlands Civic Centre multi-exit complex means he was not at the designated boarding point, and only the 34 m closest approach at 22:42:45 (F1) approaches it.

A four-minute stationary period 40 m from pickup (F3) does not satisfy NS-1 (iii), which requires waiting in range *after* the arrival confirmation; with no arrival confirmation on the record (F6), the clock NS-1 (iii) measures never started.

The 9 min 50 s from acceptance to cancellation (F4) is irrelevant because NS-1 conditions on the driver's arrival confirmation, not on elapsed time since matching; the rider's complaint wording is not contradicted by any opposite system record, and NS-2 puts the full refund on a single failed condition.
Politeness in the chat (F9, F10, F11) is not an element of NS-1 and cures no missing record; the standard for the fee is the arrival confirmation in F6, not the driver's tone.
Agreed that the amount is the published $6.61 with no surge (F7, F8); the dispute is not quantum but entitlement — NS-2 refunds that exact $6.61 because NS-1's condition (i) fails (F6).

This is the whole case: the record itself establishes the failure (F6), the driver admits it (F12), and a post-hoc statement admitting a forgotten button cannot reverse a missing system record; NS-2 applies mechanically once any NS-1 condition fails.

The rider does not seek a fraud or abuse finding against this driver; she seeks only the $6.61 refund that the missing arrival record triggers under NS-2, so the account histories (F16, F17) do not bear on the outcome.
The rider does not allege any safety event; nothing in the chat is relied on as a threat (F9, F10, F11), so SAFE-1 raises no issue and the case stays with the ordinary NS-1/NS-2 analysis.

Accepted that the fee can only rest on the no-show branch: the driver cancelled (F4) and the only fee on record is the $6.61 (F7), so the question is purely whether NS-1's substance is met, and the physical record shows it is.

Conceded on the record: the timeline shows driver_pressed_here_at is null and no automatic arrival was logged (F6), so NS-1(i) is not literally satisfied — this is the one defect in the driver's conduct, not a dispute about the facts.

Conceded: the driver's statement admits he forgot the button (F12) and cannot itself create the missing record (F6); but that omission is procedural only, and the GPS record independently shows the arrival and the wait the button would have attested (F1, F2, F3).

Denied that NS-2 follows: NS-2 is engaged only where the substance of NS-1 fails, and here the substance is established — closest approach 34 m (F1), arrival within 200 m at 22:41:30 with 5 min 20 s inside the radius (F2) and an unbroken 4 min 0 s stationary wait 40 m from pickup from 22:42:50 to 22:46:50 (F3) — so no fee is refundable on the record.

No contest, and it is the rider's own claim: the driver was at the pickup area from 22:41:30 and stayed 5 min 20 s within 200 m (F2) and messaged the vehicle identity at 22:43 (F9); the only reason the trip ended is that a second rider was not at the pickup point when the wait period expired, and the rider's own words 'I was on my way down' confirm she had not arrived.

Agreed the chat record is complete and timestamped (F11, F9, F10); for the same reason there is no G12 gap to send to a human, and the only remaining question is the legal effect of the missing button, which the driver accepts.

Profiles cut the driver's way, not the rider's: the rider has 1 dispute in 90 days with 0 upheld (F16) and the driver has 4.7 years, rating 4.87 and 951 trips in 90 days with 0 disputes upheld (F17), so no account action is warranted against this driver and profile facts cannot decide the fee question.
